title: IAPP CIPP/E
summary: The Certified Information Privacy Professional Europe (CIPP/E) is an International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP) credential for people who must apply European data protection law at work. It sits at a professional level and suits lawyers, compliance officers, privacy analysts, security staff and anyone advising on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and related European rules. It proves to an employer that you know the legal framework, the duties it places on organisations, and how those duties are met in practice. The exam is multiple choice and tests ten published knowledge areas that cover the regulatory background, key principles, individual rights, and compliance across borders and across the technology lifecycle. Typical roles include privacy analyst, data protection officer support, compliance manager and security consultant. This is an independent study guide that is not official IAPP material; the domain structure follows the published outline, so check the vendor's current version before booking.

beginner.definition: The Certified Information Privacy Professional Europe (CIPP/E) is a certification from the International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP). It shows that you understand European data protection law. The main law it covers is the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
beginner.whyItMatters: Every company that handles data about people in Europe must follow the GDPR. Someone in the company has to know those rules well. This certificate proves that you are that person. It is widely recognised, so it helps you move into privacy and compliance roles. It also works well beside a security certification.
howItWorks: Read the official IAPP exam outline, which lists the ten knowledge areas that the exam covers.
Learn the basic ideas of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), such as personal data and lawful basis.
Study the rights that people have, for example access, correction and erasure.
Learn how one company transfers data to another country and what extra steps the law requires.
Practise short case questions, because the exam asks you to apply the law and not just recall it.
The exam is multiple choice, taken at a test centre or online, and you may buy official training material or study alone.
beginner.example: Picture an online shop in Germany that sends customer names to a call centre in another country. The law does not ban this, but it does set conditions. The shop must have a lawful reason to use the data, tell customers what happens to it, and put a contract in place with the call centre. A CIPP/E holder reads that arrangement, finds the gaps, and explains the steps the shop must take. That is the daily work behind the certificate.
takeaways: CIPP/E is a legal and compliance certification, so expect reading and careful reasoning about rules.
Learn the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) as a system of duties, not as a list of facts.
Practise case questions early, because they are where most candidates lose marks.

objectives: Explain the origins and structure of European data protection law and how it is enforced
Apply the main principles of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to real processing
Identify a lawful basis for using personal data and record the choice clearly
Advise on the rights of individuals and on the duties that answer those rights
Plan the steps required when personal data is sent to another country
Judge when an assessment or a notification to a regulator is required

chapters.title: Origins and structure of European data protection law
objectives: Trace how European data protection law developed after the Second World War
Explain the role of the Council of Europe, the European Union and the Charter of Fundamental Rights
Describe how the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) replaced earlier national laws
Name the main European bodies that guide and enforce data protection
Explain how national regulators and courts work together on cross border cases

chapters.title: Scope and key terms of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
objectives: Decide what counts as personal data and as sensitive personal data
Explain the ideas of controller, processor and data subject in a given situation
Apply the rules to organisations based outside Europe that serve European people
Tell the difference between anonymised data and pseudonymised data
Recognise which activities fall outside the scope of the law

chapters.title: Principles of data protection
objectives: Apply lawfulness, fairness and transparency to a described processing activity
Limit collection to what is adequate, relevant and necessary
Judge whether stored data is kept for longer than the purpose requires
Check that data is accurate and kept up to date
Explain how accountability is shown to a regulator

chapters.title: Lawful bases for processing
objectives: Choose a lawful basis such as consent, contract, legal duty or legitimate interest
Test whether consent is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous
Apply the extra conditions for sensitive data
Balance legitimate interests against the rights of the individual
Record and review the lawful basis when the purpose changes

chapters.title: Transparency and privacy information
objectives: Draft a privacy notice that a normal reader can understand
State what information must be given and when it must be given
Explain how information is provided when data comes from another source
Describe the limited exceptions to the duty to inform
Check that layered notices and icons do not hide important facts

chapters.title: Rights of the individual
objectives: Handle a subject access request inside the legal time limit
Apply the rights to correction, erasure, restriction and objection
Explain the right to data portability and when it applies
Recognise when an automated decision needs human review
Describe the limits that can apply to a right in a specific case

chapters.title: Security of personal data
objectives: Describe the duty to keep personal data secure using suitable measures
List the information a breach notification must contain
Decide when a breach must be reported to the regulator and to individuals
Explain how processors must support the security duties of controllers
Recognise common causes of personal data breaches

chapters.title: Accountability duties of the controller
objectives: Carry out a data protection impact assessment for high risk processing
Keep records of processing activities that a regulator can review
Decide when a data protection officer must be appointed
Write contracts that set out the duties of a processor
Explain how codes of conduct and certification support accountability

chapters.title: International data transfers
objectives: Explain why a transfer to another country needs extra protection
Apply an adequacy decision when one exists
Use standard contractual clauses and assess the risks in the destination country
Describe the limited exceptions that allow a transfer without other tools
Advise a business on keeping transfer records up to date

chapters.title: Compliance across the employment and technology lifecycle
objectives: Advise on monitoring of employees and on handling human resources data
Apply data protection rules to direct marketing and online advertising
Describe how cookies and similar tools require consent
Assess new technology such as cloud services and artificial intelligence
Explain how data protection duties continue when a service is outsourced or ends
